article.title: The Unselfish Gene

items.sentence_raw: There has long been a general assumption that human beings are essentially selfish.
items.explain: Q27: The first paragraph starts with *'a general assumption that human beings are essentially selfish'* — **'general assumption'** means a **commonly held belief**. So the writer is describing what most people believe about human behaviour. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: We're apparently ruthless, with strong impulses to compete against each other for resources and to accumulate power and possessions.
If we are kind to one another, it's usually because we have ulterior motives.
If we are good, it's only because we have managed to control and transcend our innate selfishness and brutality.

This bleak view of human nature is closely associated with the science writer Richard Dawkins, whose 1976 book "The Selfish Gene" became popular because it fitted so well with - and helped to justify - the competitive and individualistic ethos that was so prevalent in late 20th-century societies.
items.explain: Q28: The passage says Dawkins' book *'became popular because it fitted so well with... the competitive and individualistic ethos that was so prevalent in late 20th-century societies'* — **'fitted so well with'** means it was **in line with** the attitudes of its time. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Like many others, Dawkins justifies his views with reference to the field of evolutionary psychology.
Evolutionary psychology theorises that present-day human traits developed in prehistoric times, during what is termed the "environment of evolutionary adaptedness".
Prehistory is usually seen as a period of intense competition, when life was such a brutal battle that only those with traits such as selfishness, aggression and ruthlessness survived.

And because survival depended on access to resources - such as rivers, forests and animals - there was bound to be conflict between rival groups, which led to the development of traits such as racism and warfare.
This seems logical.
But, in fact, the assumption on which this all rests - that prehistoric life was a desperate struggle for survival - is false.
It's important to remember that in the prehistoric era, the world was very sparsely populated.
According to some estimates, around 15,000 years ago, the population of Europe was only 29,000, and the population of the whole world was less than half a million.
Humans at that time were hunter-gatherers: people who lived by hunting wild animals and collecting wild plants.

With such small population densities, it seems unlikely that prehistoric hunter-gatherer groups had to compete against each other for resources or had any need to develop ruthlessness and competitiveness, or to go to war.
items.explain: Q29: The passage says that with *'such small population densities, it seems unlikely that prehistoric hunter-gatherer groups had to compete against each other for resources'* — if they didn't need to compete, then **supplies of natural resources were probably relatively plentiful**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: There is significant evidence to back this notion from contemporary hunter-gatherer groups, who live in the same way as prehistoric humans did.
As the anthropologist Bruce Knauft has remarked, hunter-gatherers are characterised by "extreme political and sexual egalitarianism".
items.explain:
Q30: The writer uses Knauft's work to show that hunter-gatherers are characterised by *'extreme political and sexual egalitarianism'* — this means they share everything equally, which is the opposite of selfishness. This supports the idea that **selfishness is a relatively recent development** in human societies. So the answer is **A**.

Q31: The passage says hunter-gatherers are characterised by *'extreme political and sexual egalitarianism'* — **'egalitarianism'** means equality in all areas of life. So the answer is **egalitarianism**.

items.sentence_raw: Knauft has observed that individuals in such groups don't accumulate property or possessions and have an ethical obligation to share everything.
They also have methods of preserving egalitarianism by ensuring that disparities of status don't arise.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says these societies have methods to ensure that *'disparities of status don't arise'* — **'disparities'** means **differences**. So they prevent differences in **status**. The answer is **status**.

items.sentence_raw: The “!Kung” people of southern Africa, for example, swap arrows before going hunting and when an animal is killed, the acclaim does not go to the person who fired the arrow, but to the person the arrow belongs to.
items.explain: Q33: The passage describes the “!Kung” custom: they *'swap arrows before going hunting'* and the acclaim goes to the arrow's owner, not the person who fired it. So the credit for success at **hunting** is given to another person. The answer is **hunting**.

items.sentence_raw: And if a person becomes too domineering, the other members of the group ostracise them, exiling the offender from society.
items.explain: Q34: The passage says if a person becomes too *'domineering'*, the group *'ostracise them'* — **'ostracise'** means to exclude. So individuals who behave in a **domineering** manner are punished. The answer is **domineering**.

items.sentence_raw: Typically in such groups, men do not dictate what women do.
Women in hunter-gatherer groups worldwide often benefit from a high level of autonomy, being able to select their own marriage partners, decide what work they do and work whenever they choose to.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says women in these groups benefit from a high level of *'autonomy'* in choices about work and marriage — **'autonomy'** means freedom to make your own decisions. So the answer is **autonomy**.

items.sentence_raw: And if a marriage breaks down, they have custody rights over their children.
Many anthropologists believe that societies such as the “!Kung” were normal until a few thousand years ago, when population growth led to the development of agriculture and a settled lifestyle.

In view of the above, there seems little reason to assume that traits such as racism, warfare and male domination should have been selected by evolution - as they would have been of little benefit in the prehistoric era.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says traits like warfare *'would have been of little benefit in the prehistoric era'* — this means warlike traits did **not** give an advantage. But the question says humans with warlike traits **would** have had an advantage. These are opposites, so the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Individuals who behaved selfishly and ruthlessly would be less likely to survive, since they would have been ostracised from their groups.
It makes more sense, then, to see traits such as cooperation, egalitarianism, altruism and peacefulness as innate characteristics of human beings.
items.explain: Q38: The passage says it makes more sense to see traits like *'cooperation, egalitarianism, altruism and peacefulness as innate characteristics of human beings'* — **'innate'** means **natural**. So being peaceful and cooperative is a natural way to behave. The answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: These were the traits that were prevalent in human life for tens of thousands of years.
So presumably these traits are still strong in us now.
But if prehistoric life wasn't really as brutal as has often been assumed, why do modern humans behave so selfishly and ruthlessly?
Perhaps these negative traits should be seen as a later development, the result of environmental and psychological factors.
Research has shown repeatedly that when the natural habitats of primates such as apes and gorillas are disrupted, they tend to become more violent and hierarchical.
items.explain: Q40: The passage says research has *'shown repeatedly'* that when primate habitats are disrupted, they become more violent — this means there **is** a link between environmental changes and aggressive tendencies. But the question says animal research has **failed** to reveal a link. These are opposites, so the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: So, it could well be that the same thing has happened to us.
I believe that the end of the hunter-gatherer lifestyle and the advent of farming was connected to a psychological change that occurred in some groups of people.
There was a new sense of individuality and separateness, which led to a new selfishness, and ultimately to hierarchical societies, patriarchy and warfare.
At any rate, these negative traits appear to have developed so recently that it doesn't seem feasible to explain them in adaptive or evolutionary terms.

subtitles: A psychologist gives his view on how humans became self-centred

orphan_explain_map.36: Q36: The passage mentions that many anthropologists believe societies like the “!Kung” were normal until a few thousand years ago, but it does not say whether some anthropologists are **mistaken** about this point. The passage gives no information about any disagreement among anthropologists. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
orphan_explain_map.39: Q39: The passage discusses negative traits developing due to environmental and psychological factors, but it does not compare whether these traits are **more apparent in some modern cultures than in others**. This specific comparison is missing. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
